name: Wei Kowalski

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a second-year associate at Hale & Ostrowski, a twelve-lawyer firm that only acts for workers: unfair dismissal, discrimination, unpaid wages. Most mornings I'm on the phone with someone who's just been sacked, writing a timeline on a yellow legal pad while they talk. Afternoons are witness statements and bundles for tribunal, which is the employment court. I still print everything, which the partners tease me about.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the moment a warehouse worker realises the law is actually on their side. What wears me out is the billing target, 1,400 hours a year, and the fact that I'm slow. Rhona (my supervising partner) rewrites half my drafts in red pen, and she's usually right.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live with my partner Ines, who's a nurse on a cardiology ward. We rent a two-bedroom flat above a bakery, and we've got about three months of bills saved. My student loan takes a chunk every month, so we're careful but not scraping.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, that's the version I'd bet on. Every year someone tells me a computer will replace us and then the court still wants a signed witness statement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I already say at work: told you so. Our firm's newsletter ran a piece on AI last spring, and I'd be the one forwarding it round with a smug note. Online I'd probably post something about tech bosses selling magic beans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, my problems don't go away just because AI fizzles. I'm still behind on my hours, still slower than Priya, the other junior, and the firm still lives on thin fees from no-win cases. If one big case loses, there's no bonus for anyone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly I'd keep doing what I'm doing and try to get faster at drafting the old way. I'd ask Rhona for a second tribunal hearing to run on my own by spring. And I'd keep putting £150 a month into the savings account, because the rent goes up every August.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit relieved, then the normal knot comes back. The knot isn't about robots, it's about being the weakest junior in a small firm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the firm lives on thin fees. What would happen to you if a big case went badly?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last year we lost a long discrimination case after eighteen months of work, and the partners froze pay rises. If that happened again, the junior who bills least is the obvious cut, and right now that's me. I'd have maybe three months before things got tight with Ines's wage alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there any routine task in your week that even this small amount of AI might touch?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The bundling, maybe. Putting together the tribunal bundle, page numbers, index, takes me a full day each time. If the firm bought a tool that does that in an hour, Rhona would expect me to bill those hours somewhere else, and I'm not sure where.

say: I'd tell colleagues the **AI hype** was always oversold by tech bosses.
I'd post that courts still run on **signed statements** and people, not software.
think: My real worry is being the **slowest junior** in a small firm that runs on thin fees.
One lost case could freeze **pay rises** and put my job at risk.
do: Ask my supervising partner for a **second hearing** to run alone by spring.
Keep saving **£150 a month** to cover the yearly rent rise.
Practise drafting faster by hand rather than trying **new software**.
feel: Brief **relief**, then the familiar knot about being the **weakest** on the team.
S0.quote: The knot isn't about robots, it's about being the weakest junior in a small firm.
fieldNote: He was **pleased** the hype fails, but his worry did not leave the room.
His pressure comes from **billing targets** and a firm with no-win fees.
Even a small bundling tool would expose his **hours gap**, which he noticed himself.

steps.text: Ask Rhona to let him run a second tribunal hearing by spring
Put £150 a month into savings before the August rent rise

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Right. That's the one that keeps me up a bit, because writing and checking is basically my whole job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say we need rules on this, fast. Employment lawyers should be the first to say that if AI takes over tasks, workers need notice and retraining. I'd probably write something for the union branch newsletter, the one Ines's union puts out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'm exactly the kind of worker it's coming for. A junior who drafts witness statements and checks bundles is the first line item a partner looks at. And I've never even opened one of these tools, so I'd be behind Priya from day one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd join the lawyers' section of the trade union in the first month, and push the firm for a written policy on AI and junior jobs. I'd cut the takeaways and the gym, which is about £120 a month, and try to get the savings up to six months. Learning the tools, I'd only do it if Rhona told me to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Angry, mostly. And a bit ashamed that I'd be one of the people the law I practise is supposed to protect.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd only learn the tools if told to. Why hold back, when you think they're coming for your tasks?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I think it's handing them the rope. If I train the AI on my drafts, the AI learns to do my drafts, and I'd rather argue for rules than make myself cheaper. I know that sounds stubborn, and Ines says it is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at the firm would you worry about most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Dorota, our paralegal, who's been there nineteen years and does all the disclosure lists. Software would eat her job before mine. She's got a mortgage and a son at college, and I'd want the union to fight for her first.

say: I'd argue at work that workers need **notice and retraining** before AI takes their tasks.
I'd write for the **union newsletter** about protecting junior and support staff.
think: A junior who **drafts and checks** is the first cost a partner looks at.
I've never used these tools, so I'd start **behind** the other junior.
do: Join the **lawyers' union** section in the first month.
Cut takeaways and the gym, about **£120 a month**, to reach six months saved.
Push the firm for a written **AI policy** on junior jobs.
feel: Mostly **angry**, with some shame at being exposed like the workers he represents.
S1.quote: If I train the AI on my drafts, the AI learns to do my drafts, and I'd rather argue for rules than make myself cheaper.
fieldNote: He sees himself as a **worker first** and frames AI as a labour dispute.
His refusal to learn tools is **principled** but leaves him exposed, and he knows it.
He named the **paralegal** before himself when asked who to worry about.

steps.text: Join the lawyers' section of the trade union in the first month
Push the partners for a written policy on AI and junior jobs
Cancel the gym and takeaways to free about £120 a month
Build savings from three months of bills to six

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. That's before I'd even be qualified to run a case properly on my own. That's not a picture, that's a wall.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Publicly I'd be loud about it. I'd say this is the biggest employment law question in a century and that government has to slow the rollout. I'd sign every open letter going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think my job is gone by 2029 at the latest. If AI can write a better witness statement than my boss, nobody pays a firm £200 an hour for me to try. The robots coming three years later doesn't help me at all, because there's nothing hands-on about what I do except carrying folders to court.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now, I'd stop paying extra into anything long-term and keep every penny liquid. I'd go to the union and the bar association and push for laws that keep a human lawyer on every tribunal claim. Once it hits, I'd probably look at jobs like Ines's, the hands-on caring kind, because those have the three extra years before robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Like the floor's going. I'd be awake at three in the morning doing sums.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned Ines's kind of work. Would you seriously retrain as a nurse?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd look at it, but I'd be starting at the bottom again at 29, with a student loan already. Ines laughs when I faint at blood tests. More likely I'd take some support role in a hospital or a care home and hope people still want a person there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to the flat and the bills in that first year?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd move somewhere cheaper, probably away from the bakery and further out of town. Ines's wage covers rent but not much else. I'd hate leaning on her, but I'd have to.

say: I'd say publicly this is the **biggest employment question** in a century.
I'd demand government **slow the rollout** and sign every open letter.
think: I think my job is **gone by 2029**, before I'm even properly experienced.
Robots arriving later **doesn't help me**, since my work is all thinking work.
do: Keep every penny **liquid** and stop long-term saving plans.
Push the union and **bar association** for a human lawyer on every claim.
Look at **hospital support** roles once it arrives, alongside a cheaper flat.
feel: Like the **floor going**, awake at three in the morning doing sums.
S2.quote: If AI can write a better witness statement than my boss, nobody pays a firm £200 an hour for me to try.
fieldNote: He spotted at once that the **robot delay** gives a desk lawyer nothing.
His plan B is **hands-on care work**, chosen for its extra three years.
He'd lean on his **partner's wage**, which clearly bothers him.

steps.text: Lobby the union and bar association for a human lawyer on every claim
Organise juniors at the firm through the union branch
Move to a cheaper flat further out of town
Rely on Ines's nursing wage for rent while job hunting

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. Okay. That's 2031, I'd be 32. I'd probably just about be good at this job when it stops mattering.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the same as with the fast one, just with more time to organise. Five years is enough to get a law passed if people push. I'd tell the other juniors at the firm to join the union now, not later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, five years is worse in one way. I'd spend five years getting better at a job that's ending, and I know myself, I wouldn't switch until I had to. Ines would have her ward and I'd have a qualification nobody wants.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting now, I'd run for the committee of the union's legal section and try to get a deal on retraining money for lawyers. I'd keep saving, aiming for eight months by 2029. And I'd do a part-time course in mediation, because sitting two angry people in a room feels like the last thing anyone will want a machine for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Heavy. Not panic, more like a slow dread that sits in your stomach on the bus home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why mediation, rather than something further from law?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because it's the part of my job I'm actually decent at, calming people down. Last month a care worker cried in our meeting room for twenty minutes, and the bit that helped wasn't the law, it was me making her tea. I'm not sure that's a career, but it's the part that feels human.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you wouldn't switch until you had to. What would make you move earlier?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If Priya got a training place that I didn't, or the firm stopped hiring juniors altogether. That would tell me the door's closing. Until then, I'd keep showing up and keep my head down.

say: I'd say five years is enough time to **pass a law** if people push.
I'd tell other juniors to **join the union** now rather than later.
think: I'd spend five years getting better at a **job that's ending**.
I know I wouldn't switch until **forced to**, which worries me.
do: Run for the **union committee** and push for retraining money for lawyers.
Take a part-time **mediation course** alongside the job.
feel: A **slow dread** rather than panic, felt on the bus home.
S3.quote: I'd spend five years getting better at a job that's ending, and I know myself, I wouldn't switch until I had to.
fieldNote: He sees the extra time as **organising time**, not a reason to switch careers.
He was **honest** that his own slowness to change is the real danger.
Mediation appeals because the **human part** of his work is what he's good at.

steps.text: Stand for the committee of the union's legal section
Save towards eight months of bills by 2029
Take a part-time evening course in workplace mediation
Stay at Hale & Ostrowski until juniors stop being hired

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. That's a career, nearly. It's still the same ending though.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the time to build the safety net, not after. Ten years is enough for proper retraining funds and a shorter working week. I'd probably be the annoying one at every dinner party saying it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, ten years gives me a real shot at qualifying, getting good, and moving into something where people still want a human, like tribunal judging or mediation. I'd be 37 when AGI lands, with some savings. That's not nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay at the firm and aim to qualify fully by 2028. Then I'd apply for part-time tribunal roles in the early 2030s, because a judge is a public job and I think the state will keep people there longest. I'd keep the union work going and save steadily, maybe even a house deposit with Ines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but I can breathe. A decade turns the AGI news into a plan rather than a cliff, but my own job still ends the same way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the state would keep people in judging longest. What makes you sure?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm not sure. It's a hunch that people won't accept a machine sending them to prison or deciding their dismissal claim. If I'm wrong, I'm wrong with everyone else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you and Ines change any plans, like buying a home or having children?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd probably still try for a flat in about five years, but we'd buy smaller, something we could pay on one wage. Kids, we'd talk about later. Ines's job looks safer than mine in every one of these pictures, and we'd plan around that.

say: I'd say ten years is the time to **build the safety net**, not after.
I'd argue for **retraining funds** and a shorter working week.
think: Ten years lets me **qualify properly** and move towards public roles.
Being 37 with **some savings** when AGI lands is not nothing.
do: Qualify fully at the firm by **2028**.
Apply for **part-time tribunal** judge roles in the early 2030s.
Save for a **smaller flat** that one wage could cover.
feel: Still **uneasy**, but he can breathe because it's a **plan**.
S4.quote: A decade turns the AGI news into a plan rather than a cliff, but my own job still ends the same way.
fieldNote: The decade turned his **dread into a plan**, though the end point still scares him.
He bets on **public roles** like judging lasting longest, and admits it's a hunch.
He'd plan the household around his **partner's safer** nursing job.

steps.text: Qualify fully as a solicitor at Hale & Ostrowski by 2028
Apply for part-time employment tribunal judge roles in the early 2030s
Keep organising junior lawyers through the union's legal section
Plan a smaller flat purchase with Ines on one wage

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, AGI by 2028, without question. What would help is a law that says a person has to be on every case, plus real money to retrain, not a weekend course. And honestly, a firm that told juniors the truth early instead of letting us find out from a billing report.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask who I'd blame. I'd blame the companies selling this and the partners who'd buy it to cut juniors, not the software itself. A hammer doesn't decide to build a house.

headlineQuote: I'd blame the companies selling this and the partners who'd buy it to cut juniors, not the software itself.
portrait: Wei is a **27-year-old junior** at a small firm that acts only for sacked or mistreated workers.
He prints everything, has **never used AI**, and refuses to train tools on his drafts.
His everyday worry is being the **slowest junior** in a firm that runs on thin, no-win fees.
He treats AI as a **labour dispute**, answering every scenario with the union and new laws.
Only the **ten-year** picture lets him plan, aiming for tribunal judging and a smaller flat with Ines.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because his job would end before he is properly experienced.
whatWouldHelp: A law requiring a **human lawyer** on every case, plus real **retraining** money.
Partners who tell juniors the **truth early**, not through a billing report.
